A Unified Framework for Critical Scaling
of Inverse Temperature in Self-Attention

Tomohiro Hayase Affiliation: AIST    Ryo Karakida Affiliation: AIST
Abstract

Length-dependent logit rescaling is widely used to stabilize long-context self-attention, but existing analyses and methods suggest conflicting inverse-temperature laws for the context length nn, ranging from (log⁡n)1/2(\log n)^{1/2} to log⁡n\log n and (log⁡n)2(\log n)^{2}. We provide a general theory showing that the desirable scale is determined by the gap-counting function NnN_{n} of each attention row. Counting how many competitors lie within each gap from the maximum, we define an upper-tail accumulation scale and prove that it gives the critical inverse-temperature scale for softmax concentration: below this scale, the top competitors remain unseparated, whereas above it, the attention entropy collapses. This framework unifies prior scaling laws as different NnN_{n} and yields a direct diagnostic for attention-score families, from idealized theoretical models to more practical transformers.

1 Introduction

Self-attention (Vaswani et al., 2017) is a central component of modern deep learning systems. To understand the mechanism of self-attention, theoretical studies have been actively developed. One standard approaches in theoretical analysis is to take large-degree-of-freedom limits, such as the limits of large embedding dimension and large number of heads (Hron et al., 2020; Bordelon et al., 2024; Sakai et al., 2025). In particular, motivated by the practical importance of inference with long contexts, recent work has begun to explore the infinite-context-length limit. For example, long contexts can induce token clustering as metastable states (Geshkovski et al., 2025; Bruno et al., 2025), as well as rank collapse (Nait Saada et al., 2025). Moreover, increasing the inverse temperature with the context length changes the phase from rank collapse to entropy collapse, with a critical scaling separating the two regimes (Giorlandino and Goldt, 2026; Chen et al., 2025).

Despite this progress, our understanding of the desirable scaling for long contexts is limited. The prior theory has identified critical inverse-temperature scalings only in restricted stochastic and deterministic settings, such as Gaussian-logit (i.e., random-energy-style) analyses and equicorrelated self-attention models (Giorlandino and Goldt, 2026; Chen et al., 2025). In practice, inverse temperatures that increase with the context length are also widely used to avoid the instability of inference for long contexts (Bai et al., 2023; Nakanishi, 2025; Peng et al., 2023). As reviewed in ??, these mechanisms can be placed on a common logarithmic-exponent scale, but the resulting exponents are not consistent across models and arguments. This suggests that the exponent is not determined by context length alone. What is missing is a principle that identifies, from the attention scores themselves, the scale at which softmax changes regime.

This paper develops such a principle through a deterministic gap-counting framework. Instead of organizing an attention row by ordinal rank, we count how many competitors lie within each score gap from the maximum. The exponential growth rate of this counting curve defines a row-wise critical scale, the upper-tail accumulation scale (??). Our main theorem shows that this scale controls the inverse-temperature scale separating the diffuse and concentrated softmax regimes for arbitrary deterministic score families, without assuming Gaussian logits, independent scores, random initialization, or a special token construction.

The main contribution is a unified gap-counting framework: the cumulative function Nn​(t)N_{n}(t) explains both idealized theoretical models and actual transformers, and yields a calibration principle for the inverse-temperature exponent. The upper-tail accumulation scale Λn\Lambda_{n} keeps softmax away from both non-separation of the top competitors and entropy collapse, so any non-degenerate logarithmic schedule has ξβ=ξΛ\xi_{\beta}=\xi_{\Lambda} (??); existing temperature rules become different NnN_{n} and hence different ξΛ\xi_{\Lambda}, with the legacy βn∝log⁡n\beta_{n}\propto\log n as the ξΛ=1\xi_{\Lambda}=1 slice. In two complementary settings (inference-time β\beta-sweep at extrapolation lengths and training-time learning of an inverse-temperature vector), ξ^Λ\hat{\xi}_{\Lambda} read directly from attention scores aligns with the empirical optimum ξβ∗\xi_{\beta}^{*}. ?? presents the motivating sweeps, and ?? develops the deterministic theory and applies its empirical readings to concrete self-attention scores.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Notation

Let the context length be nn. For n≥2n\geq 2, let zn,1,…,zn,n∈ℝz_{n,1},\dots,z_{n,n}\in\mathbb{R}. The softmax probability of token jj at inverse temperature β>0\beta>0 is pn,j​(β):=eβ​zn,j/∑ℓ=1neβ​zn,ℓp_{n,j}(\beta):=e^{\beta z_{n,j}}/\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}e^{\beta z_{n,\ell}}. The concrete instance we have in mind is a fixed-query self-attention row of the standard scaled dot-product form (Vaswani et al., 2017),

zn,j=⟨WnQ​xn,in,WnK​xn,j⟩dqk,n=⟨qn,in,kn,j⟩dqk,n,z_{n,j}=\frac{\langle W_{n}^{Q}x_{n,i_{n}},\,W_{n}^{K}x_{n,j}\rangle}{\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{qk},n}}}=\frac{\langle q_{n,i_{n}},k_{n,j}\rangle}{\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{qk},n}}}, (2.1)

with token embeddings xn,j∈ℝdnx_{n,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{n}}, weight matrices WnQ,WnK∈ℝdqk,n×dnW_{n}^{Q},W_{n}^{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{qk},n}\times d_{n}}, query/key vectors qn,i:=WnQ​xn,iq_{n,i}:=W_{n}^{Q}x_{n,i}, kn,j:=WnK​xn,jk_{n,j}:=W_{n}^{K}x_{n,j}, and a fixed query index ini_{n}. The theory below uses only the resulting score sequence (zn,j)j(z_{n,j})_{j}, so the embedding-weight factorization is absorbed into q,kq,k from ?? onward. For positive sequences, fn∼gnf_{n}\sim g_{n} means fn/gn→1f_{n}/g_{n}\to 1 and fn≍gnf_{n}\asymp g_{n} means c1​gn≤fn≤c2​gnc_{1}g_{n}\leq f_{n}\leq c_{2}g_{n} for some constants 0<c1≤c20<c_{1}\leq c_{2} and all sufficiently large nn. We study the asymptotic regime n→∞n\to\infty with β=βn\beta=\beta_{n}, and parametrise scaling laws by the exponent ξβ≥0\xi_{\beta}\geq 0 in βn≍(log⁡n)ξβ\beta_{n}\asymp(\log n)^{\xi_{\beta}}.

2.2 Related work

Prior choices for the softmax inverse temperature in self-attention each fix ξβ\xi_{\beta} a priori (??). Gaussian-logit analyses (ξβ=1/2\xi_{\beta}=1/2). Drawing an analogy with the Random Energy Model (Derrida, 1981), Giorlandino and Goldt (2026) conjecture βn≍log⁡n\beta_{n}\asymp\sqrt{\log n} as the scaling that balances rank and entropy collapse. Under a marginally Gaussian attention-logit assumption, Anson et al. (2025) derive a position-dependent multiplicative factor at≍log⁡ta_{t}\asymp\sqrt{\log t} that yields scale-invariant total attention. Explicit logarithmic temperature (ξβ=1\xi_{\beta}=1). SSMax (Nakanishi, 2025) multiplies attention logits by s​log⁡ns\log n with ss learned per head, and Qwen (Bai et al., 2023) adopts a length-dependent LogN multiplier of order log⁡n/log⁡ntrain\log n/\log n_{\mathrm{train}} outside the training window ntrainn_{\mathrm{train}}. Chen et al. (2025) prove a phase transition at βn≍log⁡n\beta_{n}\asymp\log n in a deterministic equicorrelated (“simplex”) configuration. Doubled rescaling (ξβ=2\xi_{\beta}=2). YaRN (Peng et al., 2023) multiplies both the query and key sides of the rotary embedding by a common log⁡n\log n-dependent multiplier, doubling the exponent (??). The values ξβ∈{1/2, 1, 2}\xi_{\beta}\in\{1/2,\,1,\,2\} are the only ones with widely cited mechanisms; intermediate values appear naturally once ξβ\xi_{\beta} is treated as a continuous parameter, as in our ξβ\xi_{\beta}-sweep (??) and our model-free gap-counting theory (??).

3 A minimal empirical check: ξβ=1\xi_{\beta}=1 is not universal

Prior mechanisms in ?? fix the logarithmic inverse-temperature exponent ξβ\xi_{\beta} a priori. We use the single-parameter ansatz βn=c​(log⁡n)ξβ\beta_{n}=c(\log n)^{\xi_{\beta}} only as a probe: the goal is to check whether the logarithmic choice ξβ=1\xi_{\beta}=1 is empirically forced.

?? gives two complementary checks. Three context-length quantities appear repeatedly below: the per-token context length nn of ??, the evaluation context length nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}} (the inference sliding-window size, fixed per evaluation, with n≤nevaln\leq n_{\mathrm{eval}}), and the training context length ntrainn_{\mathrm{train}} (the model’s training window). First, we evaluate the pretrained Qwen-7B-Chat at extrapolation lengths neval>ntrainn_{\mathrm{eval}}>n_{\mathrm{train}} (ntrain=8192n_{\mathrm{train}}=8192 for Qwen-7B-Chat), sweeping the inverse-temperature exponent ξβ\xi_{\beta} in the length-dependent multiplier βn=c​(log⁡n)ξβ\beta_{n}=c(\log n)^{\xi_{\beta}}, applied per token, while dynamic-NTK RoPE (??) is held fixed (the RoPE base is rescaled per nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}}). The perplexity sweep, scored on the back half of each sliding window so that every scored token is conditioned on at least n/2n/2 preceding tokens (formal definition in ??), is reported per nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}}. On both PG-19 (PG19) (Rae et al., 2020) and Proof-Pile-2 (PP2) (Azerbayev et al., 2024), ξβ=1\xi_{\beta}=1 is not a local minimum: the perplexity minima on the tested grid occur around ξβ∗∈[2,2.5]\xi_{\beta}^{*}\in[2,2.5], near the ξβ=2\xi_{\beta}=2 regime of YaRN (Peng et al., 2023). Qwen’s default log⁡n\log n scaling is therefore not optimal on the tested datasets and extrapolation lengths.

Second, the SSMax design of Nakanishi (2025) was motivated by a probe experiment in which a learnable per-context-length inverse-temperature vector trained from scratch was fit well by a1​log⁡n+a2a_{1}\log n+a_{2}. We replay this probe on GPT-124M (Radford et al., 2019) trained from scratch with the nanoGPT codebase (Karpathy, 2022), with a length-neval=1024n_{\mathrm{eval}}=1024 learnable vector βn\beta_{n} (one parameter per context position; protocol in ??) but generalize the fit to βn=a1​(log⁡n)ξβ\beta_{n}=a_{1}(\log n)^{\xi_{\beta}} and sweep ξβ\xi_{\beta}. On both SlimPajama (SP) (Soboleva et al., 2023) and OpenWebText (OWT) (Gokaslan et al., 2019), across the reported training snapshots, the least-squares MSE for n≥64n\geq 64 has its minimum at ξβ∗∈{0.40,0.50}\xi_{\beta}^{*}\in\{0.40,0.50\} across SlimPajama and OpenWebText; the SSMax choice ξβ=1\xi_{\beta}=1 is therefore not optimal even on its own motivating experiment.

Both sweeps therefore give concrete cases in which ξβ≠1\xi_{\beta}\neq 1 is preferred (full protocols, grids, companion sweeps, and per-context numerics in ??). They select different values of ξβ\xi_{\beta}, because perplexity and the learned βn\beta_{n} are different spatially-averaged observables of the same representation. ?? characterizes the general cause of softmax collapse: ξβ\xi_{\beta} is fixed by the row-wise NnN_{n} of attention scores.

4 Deterministic theory

The deterministic theory of softmax collapse is most naturally phrased in terms of how many competitors lie within a given gap of the winner, not in terms of which ordinal rank a competitor occupies: a one-step rank change can correspond to a negligible score change on one row and a large one on another, whereas increasing the gap by δ\delta always suppresses a competitor’s weight by the same factor e−β​δe^{-\beta\delta}. Grouping the softmax partition function by gap rewrites it as a transform of a cumulative gap-counting curve, and the inverse temperature at which softmax collapses is then read off the exponential growth rate of that curve, namely the upper-tail accumulation scale Λn\Lambda_{n} of ??. ?? first fixes the collapse observables against which Λn\Lambda_{n} is identified as the relevant scale.

4.1 Collapse observables and the critical scale

Definition 4.1 (Collapse observables).

Adopt the softmax probabilities pn,j​(β)p_{n,j}(\beta) from ??. The Shannon entropy is Hn(β):=−∑j=1npn,j(β)logpn,j(β)H_{n}(\beta):=-\sum_{j=1}^{n}p_{n,j}(\beta)\log p_{n,j}(\beta), and the top-two weight gap Dn​(β)D_{n}(\beta) is the difference between the largest and second-largest entries of (pn,j​(β))j=1n(p_{n,j}(\beta))_{j=1}^{n}. Along a positive deterministic sequence (βn)(\beta_{n}), we say top-two collapse holds if Dn​(βn)→0D_{n}(\beta_{n})\to 0, entropy collapse if Hn​(βn)→0H_{n}(\beta_{n})\to 0, and rank collapse if maxi,j⁡|pn,i​(βn)−pn,j​(βn)|→0\max_{i,j}\bigl|p_{n,i}(\beta_{n})-p_{n,j}(\beta_{n})\bigr|\to 0.

Definition 4.2 (Critical scale).

A positive deterministic sequence (Xn)(X_{n}) is a rank–entropy scale (RE scale) if, for every positive deterministic sequence (βn)(\beta_{n}),

βn/Xn→0⟹rank collapse,βn/Xn→∞⟹entropy collapse,\beta_{n}/X_{n}\to 0\;\Longrightarrow\;\text{rank collapse},\qquad\beta_{n}/X_{n}\to\infty\;\Longrightarrow\;\text{entropy collapse},

in the sense of ??, and a top-two–entropy scale (TE scale) if the subcritical conclusion is replaced by top-two collapse. Each is unique up to ≍\asymp when it exists.

We refer to TE and RE scales collectively as critical scales: each is a deterministic sequence that separates a subcritical regime, in which a collapse observable vanishes, from a supercritical regime in which entropy collapses. Rank collapse is the standard transformer-literature notion of convergence of an attention row toward the uniform law (1/n,…,1/n)(1/n,\dots,1/n) (Dong et al., 2021; Noci et al., 2022; Geshkovski et al., 2025), strictly stronger than top-two collapse.

The primary scale here is Λn\Lambda_{n} of ??, which ?? identifies as a critical scale (top-two/entropy sense of ??) and which inverse-temperature calibration requires (??). ?? additionally upgrades Λn\Lambda_{n} to the standard rank-collapse boundary under Cn:=Λn​Δn=αn​log⁡n→∞C_{n}:=\Lambda_{n}\Delta_{n}=\alpha_{n}\log n\to\infty (?? for the contrary case), an observable-specific refinement that does not change the calibration principle.

4.2 Counting function, upper-tail accumulation scale, and contact point

Definition 4.3 (Cumulative gap-counting function).

Set zn∗:=max1≤j≤n⁡zn,jz_{n}^{*}:=\max_{1\leq j\leq n}z_{n,j}. The cumulative gap-counting function

Nn​(t):=#⁡{j∣zn∗−zn,j≤t},t≥0,N_{n}(t):=\#\{j\mid z_{n}^{*}-z_{n,j}\leq t\},\qquad t\geq 0,

counts the indices jj with zn∗−zn,j≤tz_{n}^{*}-z_{n,j}\leq t; such an index jj is called a tt-competitor (the prefix tt is dropped when unambiguous). In the physics analogy with −zn,j-z_{n,j} as energies, the gap zn∗−zn,jz_{n}^{*}-z_{n,j} is the excitation above the ground state z=zn∗z=z_{n}^{*}, and Nn​(t)N_{n}(t) counts states with excitation energy at most tt.

The softmax probabilities of ?? factor through the normalised partition function Zn​(β):=∑j=1ne−β⁡(zn∗−zn,j)Z_{n}(\beta):=\sum_{j=1}^{n}e^{-\beta(z_{n}^{*}-z_{n,j})}, pn,j​(β)=exp⁡[−β⁡(zn∗−zn,j)]/Zn​(β),p_{n,j}(\beta)=\exp[{-\beta(z_{n}^{*}-z_{n,j})}]/Z_{n}(\beta), and integration by parts (with Nn​(0−)=0N_{n}(0^{-})=0 and e−β​t​Nn​(t)→0e^{-\beta t}N_{n}(t)\to 0 as t→∞t\to\infty) gives

Zn​(β)=β​∫0∞e−β​t​Nn​(t)​𝑑t.Z_{n}(\beta)=\beta\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\,N_{n}(t)\,dt. (4.1)

The integrand of (4.1) is e−β​t​Nn​(t)e^{-\beta t}N_{n}(t). Whether the exponential damping e−β​te^{-\beta t} outpaces the growth of Nn​(t)N_{n}(t) is captured by the envelope Nn​(t)≤eβ​tN_{n}(t)\leq e^{\beta t}, and the smallest exponent for which this envelope holds is the next definition.

Definition 4.4 (Upper-tail accumulation scale).

The upper-tail accumulation scale Λn\Lambda_{n} is the smallest exponent for which the envelope

Nn​(t)≤eΛn​t(t>0)N_{n}(t)\leq e^{\Lambda_{n}t}\qquad(t>0) (4.2)

holds, equivalently

Λn:=supt>0log⁡Nn​(t)t.\Lambda_{n}:=\sup_{t>0}\frac{\log N_{n}(t)}{t}. (4.3)

Throughout the remainder of this section, we assume Λn<+∞\Lambda_{n}<+\infty eventually in nn; the boundary case Λn=∞\Lambda_{n}=\infty (ties at the maximum, which forces log⁡Nn​(t)/t→∞\log N_{n}(t)/t\to\infty as t↓0t\downarrow 0) is deferred to ??. Under this finite-Λn\Lambda_{n} assumption the map t↦log⁡Nn​(t)/tt\mapsto\log N_{n}(t)/t is non-increasing between consecutive competitor gaps and the supremum is attained as a maximum at some positive competitor gap zn∗−zn,j>0z_{n}^{*}-z_{n,j}>0 (??).

Definition 4.5 (Contact point).

Call a positive competitor gap u=zn∗−zn,j>0u=z_{n}^{*}-z_{n,j}>0 a contact gap if log⁡Nn​(u)/u=Λn\log N_{n}(u)/u=\Lambda_{n} (the envelope N≤eΛn​tN\leq e^{\Lambda_{n}t} is attained at t=ut=u). Let Δn\Delta_{n} be the largest such gap, and define the contact accumulation exponent αn:=log⁡Nn​(Δn)/log⁡n\alpha_{n}:=\log N_{n}(\Delta_{n})/\log n. The pair (αn,Δn)(\alpha_{n},\Delta_{n}) is the (largest) contact point and satisfies the contact formula

Λn=αn​log⁡nΔn.\Lambda_{n}=\frac{\alpha_{n}\log n}{\Delta_{n}}. (4.4)

?? shows the gap-counting curve, the exponential envelope, and the contact point. The coordinate αn\alpha_{n} records the finite-nn contact count on the scale of nn, while Δn\Delta_{n} records the corresponding gap. The contact formula (4.4) is the only relation between these coordinates used below.

Theorem 4.6.

(Λn)(\Lambda_{n}) is the TE scale.

4.3 Logarithmic critical-scaling exponent

Having established that Λn\Lambda_{n} is a critical scale, we now record how its logarithmic growth rate is read from the contact coordinates of ??.

For any positive sequence (Xn)(X_{n}), if Xn≍(log⁡n)ξX_{n}\asymp(\log n)^{\xi}, then the exponent is unique when it exists: if ξ\xi and ξ′\xi^{\prime} both work, then (log⁡n)ξ−ξ′(\log n)^{\xi-\xi^{\prime}} is bounded above and below, forcing ξ=ξ′\xi=\xi^{\prime}. We call this ξ\xi the logarithmic growth exponent of (Xn)(X_{n}) and denote it ξX\xi_{X}, so that

Xn≍(log⁡n)ξX.X_{n}\asymp(\log n)^{\xi_{X}}. (4.6)

This single rule produces ξΛ,ξα,ξΔ,ξβ\xi_{\Lambda},\xi_{\alpha},\xi_{\Delta},\xi_{\beta} as instances of one family. The principal exponent of the system is ξΛ\xi_{\Lambda}, the growth exponent of the upper-tail accumulation scale Λn\Lambda_{n}.

Corollary 4.8 (Exponent-selection rule).

Under Λn≍(log⁡n)ξΛ\Lambda_{n}\asymp(\log n)^{\xi_{\Lambda}} and βn≍(log⁡n)ξβ\beta_{n}\asymp(\log n)^{\xi_{\beta}}, any schedule avoiding both top-two and entropy collapse has ξβ=ξΛ\xi_{\beta}=\xi_{\Lambda} (otherwise βn/Λn→0\beta_{n}/\Lambda_{n}\to 0 or →∞\to\infty, contradicting ??).

The contact formula (4.4) expresses ξΛ\xi_{\Lambda} in the contact coordinates of ?? as a linear combination.

Corollary 4.9 (Coordinate decomposition of ξΛ\xi_{\Lambda}).

If any two of Λn,αn,Δn\Lambda_{n},\alpha_{n},\Delta_{n} admit logarithmic growth exponents in the sense of (4.6), then so does the third, and they satisfy

ξΛ=ξα−ξΔ+1.\xi_{\Lambda}\;=\;\xi_{\alpha}-\xi_{\Delta}+1. (4.7)
Proof.

Multiplying ≍\asymp-classes in the contact formula (4.4) gives Λn=αn​(log⁡n)​Δn−1≍(log⁡n)ξα​(log⁡n)​(log⁡n)−ξΔ=(log⁡n)ξα−ξΔ+1,\Lambda_{n}=\alpha_{n}\,(\log n)\,\Delta_{n}^{-1}\;\asymp\;(\log n)^{\xi_{\alpha}}\,(\log n)\,(\log n)^{-\xi_{\Delta}}=(\log n)^{\xi_{\alpha}-\xi_{\Delta}+1}, and uniqueness of the exponent yields (4.7). Solving the contact formula for αn\alpha_{n} or Δn\Delta_{n} covers the symmetric directions. ∎

The corollary makes ξα,ξΔ\xi_{\alpha},\xi_{\Delta} first-class coordinate exponents on equal footing with ξΛ\xi_{\Lambda}, and the side of 11 on which ξΛ\xi_{\Lambda} lands is determined by the sign of ξα−ξΔ\xi_{\alpha}-\xi_{\Delta}. ?? uses this decomposition empirically.

4.4 Gap-counting on the equicorrelated configuration and a block extension

The contact formula (4.4) constrains the one-row NnN_{n} but not the configuration behind it. The deterministic equicorrelated (“simplex”) configuration of Cowsik et al. (2025), whose critical βn≍log⁡n\beta_{n}\asymp\log n was established by Chen et al. (2025), is the simplest configuration to which the framework applies; gap-counting reads ξΛ\xi_{\Lambda} off it directly. A balanced block-constant extension also tunes the contact count αn\alpha_{n}. Both body constructions take the score matrix as a symmetric Gram matrix Σn\Sigma_{n}, equivalently the self-attention score matrix (2.1) with WnQ=WnKW_{n}^{Q}=W_{n}^{K} (??); this Q=KQ=K restriction is standard in theoretical analyses of attention (Chen et al., 2025; Geshkovski et al., 2023; Arnaboldi et al., 2025). Chen et al. (2025), in particular, work with the equicorrelated Gram of identity-coupled tokens, equivalent in our notation to the WnQ=WnK=IW_{n}^{Q}=W_{n}^{K}=I specialization of (2.1). In both body constructions, Nn​(t)N_{n}(t) has at most two positive jumps. We write δn\delta_{n} for the minimum positive gap and reserve Δn\Delta_{n} for the contact gap of ??; they coincide (Δn=δn\Delta_{n}=\delta_{n}) only in the within-block-dominant case.

Equicorrelated (simplex) configuration.

With common norm ‖xi‖2=q\|x_{i}\|^{2}=q and pairwise inner product ⟨xi,xj⟩=ρ<q\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle=\rho<q, set Jn:=𝟏𝟏⊤J_{n}:=\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}, rn2:=qr_{n}^{2}:=q, Δn:=q−ρ\Delta_{n}:=q-\rho to obtain

Σnsimp:=(rn2−Δn)​Jn+Δn​In≥0.\Sigma_{n}^{\mathrm{simp}}:=(r_{n}^{2}-\Delta_{n})J_{n}+\Delta_{n}I_{n}\geq 0.

Every query has flat competitor gap Δn\Delta_{n}, so NnN_{n} jumps from 11 to nn at t=Δnt=\Delta_{n} and Λn=log⁡n/Δn\Lambda_{n}=\log n/\Delta_{n}, αn=1\alpha_{n}=1, the full-count endpoint. The βn≍log⁡n\beta_{n}\asymp\log n scaling of Chen et al. (2025) is the ξΛ=1\xi_{\Lambda}=1 slice (Δn=Θ⁡(1)\Delta_{n}=\Theta(1)); Δn=(log⁡n)1−ξΛ\Delta_{n}=(\log n)^{1-\xi_{\Lambda}} realizes any ξΛ≥0\xi_{\Lambda}\geq 0. Reading off the contact coordinates gives ξα=0\xi_{\alpha}=0 and ξΔ=1−ξΛ\xi_{\Delta}=1-\xi_{\Lambda}, which satisfy the decomposition (4.7) of ??: this configuration sits on the ξα=0\xi_{\alpha}=0 axis with ξΛ\xi_{\Lambda} entirely carried by ξΔ\xi_{\Delta}.

Two-level block-constant extension.

A balanced block-constant analogue of Σnsimp\Sigma_{n}^{\mathrm{simp}} tunes αn\alpha_{n} as well as ξΛ\xi_{\Lambda}. Fix mn∈{2,…,n}m_{n}\in\{2,\dots,n\} with mn|nm_{n}\mid n, and partition {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\} into blocks of size mnm_{n}. Let BnB_{n} be the block-membership matrix, equivalently the block-diagonal matrix with n/mnn/m_{n} diagonal blocks equal to JmnJ_{m_{n}}. For 0<δn<τn≤rn20<\delta_{n}<\tau_{n}\leq r_{n}^{2}, define

Σnblock:=δn​In+(τn−δn)​Bn+(rn2−τn)​Jn≥0.\Sigma_{n}^{\mathrm{block}}:=\delta_{n}I_{n}+(\tau_{n}-\delta_{n})B_{n}+(r_{n}^{2}-\tau_{n})J_{n}\ \geq 0. (4.8)

Positivity follows from In,Bn,Jn≥0I_{n},B_{n},J_{n}\geq 0 and the nonnegative coefficients. The entries are rn2r_{n}^{2} on the diagonal, rn2−δnr_{n}^{2}-\delta_{n} inside a block, and rn2−τnr_{n}^{2}-\tau_{n} across blocks; thus rn2r_{n}^{2} is a common score shift, while δn\delta_{n} and τn\tau_{n} are the two relevant row gaps. Consequently Nn​(t)=1N_{n}(t)=1 for 0≤t<δn0\leq t<\delta_{n}, Nn​(t)=mnN_{n}(t)=m_{n} for δn≤t<τn\delta_{n}\leq t<\tau_{n}, and Nn​(t)=nN_{n}(t)=n for t≥τnt\geq\tau_{n} (??). Hence

Λn=max⁡{log⁡mnδn,log⁡nτn}.\Lambda_{n}=\max\!\left\{\frac{\log m_{n}}{\delta_{n}},\,\frac{\log n}{\tau_{n}}\right\}. (4.9)

The smaller-gap jump dominates when log⁡mn/δn>log⁡n/τn\log m_{n}/\delta_{n}>\log n/\tau_{n}; then Δn=δn\Delta_{n}=\delta_{n} and αn=log⁡mn/log⁡n\alpha_{n}=\log m_{n}/\log n. A prescribed Λn=(log⁡n)ξΛ\Lambda_{n}=(\log n)^{\xi_{\Lambda}} is realized by taking δn=log⁡mn/(log⁡n)ξΛ\delta_{n}=\log m_{n}/(\log n)^{\xi_{\Lambda}} and τn=C​log⁡n/(log⁡n)ξΛ\tau_{n}=C\log n/(\log n)^{\xi_{\Lambda}} with C>1C>1. With mn=nβm_{n}=n^{\beta} (β∈(0,1]\beta\in(0,1]), the contact coordinates give ξα=0\xi_{\alpha}=0 and ξΔ=1−ξΛ\xi_{\Delta}=1-\xi_{\Lambda}, recovering the simplex slice on a different αn=β\alpha_{n}=\beta level. With bounded mn=m≥2m_{n}=m\geq 2, αn=log⁡m/log⁡n≍(log⁡n)−1\alpha_{n}=\log m/\log n\asymp(\log n)^{-1} gives ξα=−1\xi_{\alpha}=-1, and δn=log⁡m/(log⁡n)ξΛ≍(log⁡n)−ξΛ\delta_{n}=\log m/(\log n)^{\xi_{\Lambda}}\asymp(\log n)^{-\xi_{\Lambda}} gives ξΔ=−ξΛ\xi_{\Delta}=-\xi_{\Lambda}; both branches satisfy (4.7) (e.g. in the second branch ξα−ξΔ+1=−1−(−ξΛ)+1=ξΛ\xi_{\alpha}-\xi_{\Delta}+1=-1-(-\xi_{\Lambda})+1=\xi_{\Lambda}). The block extension is the simplest configuration in which ξα\xi_{\alpha} takes values other than 00. The reverse case has Δn=τn\Delta_{n}=\tau_{n} and αn=1\alpha_{n}=1, coinciding with the simplex endpoint. When Λn\Lambda_{n} is specified only up to ≍\asymp, we pass to block-compatible subsequences with mn|nm_{n}\mid n.

The block-constant configuration corresponds to token vectors with a hierarchical cluster structure: within each block, tokens cluster around a common centroid at within-block gap δn\delta_{n}, while distinct blocks are separated by the larger across-block gap τn\tau_{n}. Such hierarchically structured token representations are themselves an object of study, with Li et al. (2023) giving a mechanistic account of topic clustering inside trained transformers and Garnier-Brun et al. (2025) analyzing attention block structure under hierarchical filtering of the input.

5 Discussion and Conclusion

This paper asks what determines the critical scaling of inverse temperature for self-attention in the long-context limit. Our answer is that it is determined by (Λn,αn,Δn)(\Lambda_{n},\alpha_{n},\Delta_{n}). The cumulative gap-counting function Nn​(t)N_{n}(t) of ?? records how many competitors lie within each gap of the winning score, and the upper-tail accumulation scale Λn\Lambda_{n} of ?? gives the relevant scale. ?? identifies Λn\Lambda_{n} as a critical scale for arbitrary deterministic score rows; ?? sharpens this to the standard rank-collapse boundary whenever the contact-count entropy αn​log⁡n=Λn​Δn\alpha_{n}\log n=\Lambda_{n}\Delta_{n} diverges, with empirical verification on the bounded-CnC_{n} cells via ??. Thus the exponent ξβ\xi_{\beta} in βn≍(log⁡n)ξβ\beta_{n}\asymp(\log n)^{\xi_{\beta}} is not universal: any non-degenerate schedule has ξβ=ξΛ\xi_{\beta}=\xi_{\Lambda} (??), the logarithmic growth rate of Λn\Lambda_{n} in the sense of (4.6). Equivalently, the contact formula (4.4) shows that ξβ\xi_{\beta} is determined by both the contact count αn\alpha_{n} and the contact gap Δn\Delta_{n} of ??, namely ξβ=ξα−ξΔ+1\xi_{\beta}=\xi_{\alpha}-\xi_{\Delta}+1 (??). This also explains why the mechanisms in ?? give different exponents (they induce different NnN_{n}, not different universal laws), and why empirical long-context behavior can prefer values away from the legacy logarithmic choice ξβ=1\xi_{\beta}=1.

Limitations and open problem.

The main limitation of the present framework is that the score family, and hence (Λn,αn,Δn)(\Lambda_{n},\alpha_{n},\Delta_{n}), is taken as given. We do not yet derive it from the architecture, positional encoding, data distribution, or training dynamics of a concrete transformer. A natural open problem is therefore to endogenize these quantities through the dynamics of self-attention. Recent inference-time theories of recurrent or infinitely deep self-attention describe token representations as interacting particles whose empirical geometry can develop clustered, metastable, or lower-dimensional structure across depth or loop time (Geshkovski et al., 2023; Geshkovski et al., 2024; Karagodin et al., 2024; Bruno et al., 2025; Tomihari and Karakida, 2025; Rigollet, 2026). Complementary learning-time analyses show that training can progressively encode semantic, positional, or hierarchical structure into embeddings and attention maps (Li et al., 2023; Garnier-Brun et al., 2025; Arnaboldi et al., 2025). Coupling such inference-time and learning-time dynamics with the present gap-counting theory would turn Nn​(t)N_{n}(t), Λn\Lambda_{n}, and (αn,Δn)(\alpha_{n},\Delta_{n}) into observables that depend on depth, loop time, and training time, making it possible to predict how the critical inverse-temperature scale is shaped by the model and data rather than treating the score family as fixed.

Appendix A Experimental setup

This appendix collects the experimental basic setup shared across the inference-time ξ\xi-sweep of ?? and the training-time gap-exponent trajectory of ??. The per-experiment grids, seeds, ξ0\xi_{0} values, and numerical tolerances are recorded in the corresponding protocol appendices (??, ??, ??).

A.1 Datasets

The Qwen long-context ξ\xi-sweep (??) draws documents from the PG-19 (Rae et al., 2020) test split and the Proof-Pile-2 (Azerbayev et al., 2024) arXiv test split (up to 2020 per dataset per nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}}; the per-cell counts entering the perplexity averages are listed in ??). The Qwen-7B-Chat gap-counting analysis (??) uses a smaller fixed subset of these documents because the per-row analysis is heavier: 44 from PG-19 and 55 from Proof-Pile-2 enter the headline statistics of ??, which together with the (ξ0,neval,ratio)(\xi_{0},n_{\mathrm{eval}},\text{ratio}) grid produces the 774,144774{,}144 attention rows enumerated in ??. The GPT-124M training-time runs of ??, ?? are pretrained on SlimPajama (Soboleva et al., 2023) and OpenWebText (Gokaslan et al., 2019), one run per dataset.

A.2 Qwen long-context evaluation

We probe two pretrained checkpoints: Qwen-1.8B-Chat with training window ntrain=8192n_{\mathrm{train}}=8192, and Qwen-7B-Chat (3232 transformer layers, 3232 attention heads per layer) also with ntrain=8192n_{\mathrm{train}}=8192. Both keep rotary position embeddings (Su et al., 2024) on with the dynamic-NTK RoPE base schedule of Peng et al. (2023, §3.4) defined just below. On top of dynamic-NTK, we apply the legacy length-dependent multiplier

m⁡(n,ξ)=(max⁡(1,log⁡n/log⁡ntrain))ξm(n;\xi)=\bigl(\max(1,\log n/\log n_{\mathrm{train}})\bigr)^{\xi}

to the attention logits at extrapolation lengths n>ntrainn>n_{\mathrm{train}}, equivalent to the parameterization βn∝(log⁡n)ξ\beta_{n}\propto(\log n)^{\xi} for n>ntrainn>n_{\mathrm{train}} and to the no-multiplier baseline at ξ=0\xi=0; the YaRN inverse-temperature window ξ=2\xi=2 (Peng et al., 2023) corresponds to the YaRN schedule as derived in ??. The contexts nn and ξ\xi-grids vary by experiment and are recorded with the respective figures.

Dynamic-NTK RoPE.

Standard RoPE (Su et al., 2024) rotates the per-head query/key pair in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} using a fixed base θ0\theta_{0} (typically θ0=10000\theta_{0}=10000): the kk-th coordinate pair at position ii is multiplied by R(iθ0−2k/d)R(i\,\theta_{0}^{-2k/d}). The dynamic-NTK schedule of Peng et al. (2023, §3.4) (also Bai et al. 2023 for Qwen) replaces θ0\theta_{0} by a per-evaluation base θ0​s​(neval)\theta_{0}\,s(n_{\mathrm{eval}}) where, with the extrapolation ratio ρ⁡(neval):=max⁡(1,neval/ntrain)\rho(n_{\mathrm{eval}}):=\max(1,n_{\mathrm{eval}}/n_{\mathrm{train}}),

s⁡(neval):=ρ​(neval)d/(d−2).s(n_{\mathrm{eval}})\;:=\;\rho(n_{\mathrm{eval}})^{d/(d-2)}.

The base is recomputed once per inference window of size nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}} and then held fixed across positions i≤nevali\leq n_{\mathrm{eval}} inside the window. The high-frequency rotations are nearly unchanged while the low-frequency ones are stretched, so embeddings of relative offsets that exceed ntrainn_{\mathrm{train}} at evaluation time stay within the angular range the model saw during training. Throughout this paper, “dynamic-NTK RoPE” refers to this schedule, with the legacy multiplier m⁡(n,ξ)m(n;\xi) above applied as a separate inverse-temperature scalar on the attention logits.

Sliding-window perplexity.

We report back-half sliding-window perplexity: a long document is partitioned into non-overlapping windows of length nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}}, and within each window only the second half (positions j∈(neval/2,neval]j\in(n_{\mathrm{eval}}/2,n_{\mathrm{eval}}]) contributes to the loss, so every scored token is conditioned on ≥neval/2\geq n_{\mathrm{eval}}/2 preceding tokens. Concretely, with ℓ⁡(j)\ell(j) the cross-entropy of the model on the jj-th token of the window, the window contribution to log-perplexity is ∑j>neval/2ℓ⁡(j)/(neval/2)\sum_{j>n_{\mathrm{eval}}/2}\ell(j)\bigm/(n_{\mathrm{eval}}/2), averaged across windows and documents and exponentiated. This is the protocol called strict sliding-window perplexity in earlier drafts and in some external references; we drop the modifier in the body since the back-half restriction is the only convention used. The convention controls position-context confounding at extrapolation lengths neval>ntrainn_{\mathrm{eval}}>n_{\mathrm{train}}: under no-overlap windows the early positions of a window see only short prefixes, which would otherwise dominate the loss for n>ntrainn>n_{\mathrm{train}}.

A.3 GPT-124M training-time setup

GPT-124M (Radford et al., 2019) (1212 transformer layers, 1212 attention heads per layer, context length neval=1024n_{\mathrm{eval}}=1024) is trained from scratch using the nanoGPT codebase (Karpathy, 2022) in four configurations: two positional encodings (learned absolute, as in GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019); rotary (Su et al., 2024)) ×\times two pretraining datasets (SlimPajama, OpenWebText). Each configuration runs for 100,000100{,}000 iterations with checkpoints saved every 50005000 iterations; the seven milestones iter∈{0,5​k,10​k,25​k,50​k,75​k,100​k}\mathrm{iter}\in\{0,5\textrm{k},10\textrm{k},25\textrm{k},50\textrm{k},75\textrm{k},100\textrm{k}\} are the snapshots used by the body and appendix figures.

Learnable inverse-temperature vector βn\beta_{n}.

Each model carries an additional length-nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}} vector βn\beta_{n} (one parameter per context position nn) tied across layers and heads; per (layer, head) the actual attention multiplier is

βn,ℓ,h=sℓ,h​βn+bℓ,h,\beta_{n,\ell,h}=s_{\ell,h}\,\beta_{n}+b_{\ell,h}, (A.1)

with per-head scale sℓ,hs_{\ell,h} and bias bℓ,hb_{\ell,h} trained alongside βn\beta_{n}. The nn-dependence is carried entirely by βn\beta_{n}; the body’s βn\beta_{n} regression fit (??) reads βn\beta_{n} off after training and fits it to a1​(log⁡n)ξa_{1}(\log n)^{\xi}, while the gap-exponent diagnostic (??) compares raw and effective gap exponents row-wise. Unlike SSMax, which fixes βn,ℓ,h=sℓ,h​log⁡n\beta_{n,\ell,h}=s_{\ell,h}\log n with a single scalar sℓ,hs_{\ell,h} per head, here βn\beta_{n} is unconstrained at initialization and is shaped only by the training loss. The original SSMax design-rationale experiment of Nakanishi (2025) used the same unconstrained βn\beta_{n} vector and fit it by least squares to a1​log⁡n+a2a_{1}\log n+a_{2}, motivating the logarithmic constraint.

Hyperparameters.

?? records the architecture, βn\beta_{n} realization, and optimization settings shared across the four configurations, together with the four (positional encoding, dataset) pairs that distinguish them. All values are read from the training configs of the runs (n_layer, n_head, n_embd, optimizer schedule, etc.).

A.4 Compute resources

All experiments ran on academic GPU clusters equipped with NVIDIA H100 GPUs (9696 GB HBM3). Two job sizes were used: a single-GPU job (one H100) and a full-node job (eight H100s).

Qwen inference (??, ??).

The Qwen long-context ξβ\xi_{\beta} sweep (??, ??, ??) and the gap-counting attention-row capture (??) each run as single-GPU jobs. Per back-half sliding-window perplexity job (one (ξβ,dataset)(\xi_{\beta},\text{dataset}) covering all five contexts neval∈{8192,12288,16384,24576,32768}n_{\mathrm{eval}}\in\{8192,12288,16384,24576,32768\} on 2020 documents): ∼25{\sim}25 minutes wall on one H100, of which ∼5{\sim}5 minutes per context. Per attention-row gap capture job (one (ξ0,dataset,neval,doc)(\xi_{0},\text{dataset},n_{\mathrm{eval}},\text{doc})): ∼2{\sim}2 minutes wall on one H100. The full ξβ\xi_{\beta} refinement to 0.10.1 resolution on Qwen-7B-Chat used ≤60\leq 60 GPU-hours. The gap-counting capture for the body Table 2 cells, the ξ0\xi_{0}-sweep, and the ξ0\xi_{0} fixed-point refinement together used ∼10{\sim}10 additional GPU-hours on the same single-H100 budget. Total Qwen H100-hours for the content reported in this paper: ∼80{\sim}80.

nanoGPT training-time runs (??, ??).

Each of the four training-time GPT-124M runs of ?? runs as a full-node job (88 H100, distributed via torchrun with effective batch 20482048 sequences of length 10241024, walltime budget 2424 hours per run). A complete run reaches 100,000100{,}000 iterations in well under the budget; total nanoGPT training compute reported in this paper is bounded by 4​runs×24​h×8​H100=7684\,\text{runs}\times 24\,\text{h}\times 8\,\text{H100}=768 H100-hours. Per-checkpoint dump and post-processing for the seven milestone checkpoints {0,5​k,…,100​k}\{0,5\textrm{k},\ldots,100\textrm{k}\} on three evaluation seeds adds order 2020 GPU-hours.

Storage.

The Qwen full-gap safetensors at the body’s (d​s,neval,ξ0,doc)(ds,n_{\mathrm{eval}},\xi_{0},\mathrm{doc}) grid plus the off-grid points generated for the ξ0\xi_{0} fixed-point search occupy ∼150{\sim}150 GB of project-area storage; the nanoGPT checkpoint set occupies ∼30{\sim}30 GB per training run.

Preliminary work.

The headline compute above does not include preliminary ξβ\xi_{\beta}- sweep iterations on Qwen-1.8B-Chat at intermediate grid resolutions, exploratory ξ0\xi_{0} ablations, and discarded gap-capture pipelines (direct top-kk vs full sorted-gap dumps). Counting these, the full research project consumed roughly twice the headline budget, all on the same internal H100 clusters.

A.5 Reproducibility capsule

This subsection collects the environment and artifact pointers needed to reproduce the headline experiments alongside the protocols documented in ??, ??, ??, ??, ??.

Environment.

We list only the dependencies that affect the experiment outputs; the SciPy-stack analysis packages used downstream of the captured CSVs are omitted because any current version reproduces the same numerics. The Qwen long-context evaluations run under Python 3.113.11 with PyTorch 2.62.6 (CUDA 12.412.4 build), transformers 4.32.04.32.0 (the version pinned by the Qwen-7B-Chat model card and required by the bundled custom modeling file loaded with trust_remote_code=True), flash-attn 2.8.32.8.3, and einops 0.80.8 (used inside that modeling file). The GPT-124M training-time runs use Python 3.123.12 with the same PyTorch build and tiktoken 0.120.12 (GPT-2 BPE). All experiments run on NVIDIA H100 (9696 GB HBM3) GPUs.

Artifact identifiers.

The Qwen checkpoints are the public Qwen/Qwen-7B-Chat and Qwen/Qwen-1_8B-Chat HuggingFace releases used as published (no fine-tuning); their bundled config.json reports transformers_version 4.32.04.32.0, fixing the modeling-file revision the trust_remote_code loader executes. The training-time runs are built on the public nanoGPT codebase (Karpathy, 2022) (snapshot from spring 20262026) with the length-nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}} learnable βn\beta_{n} vector inserted as in (A.1). The text corpora are the deepmind/pg19, EleutherAI/proof-pile-2 (arXiv subset), cerebras/SlimPajama-627B, and Skylion007/openwebtext HuggingFace dataset releases as of the experiment dates; tokenization uses each model’s bundled tokenizer (Qwen’s BPE for the Qwen evaluations, GPT-2 BPE via tiktoken for the nanoGPT training and validation passes).

Modification surface.

The Qwen-side per-token multiplier m⁡(n,ξ)=(max⁡(1,log⁡n/log⁡ntrain))ξm(n;\xi)=\bigl(\max(1,\log n/\log n_{\mathrm{train}})\bigr)^{\xi} of ?? is applied after the per-head dot-product score zn,j=⟨𝐪n,in,𝐤n,j⟩/dq​kz_{n,j}=\langle\mathbf{q}_{n,i_{n}},\mathbf{k}_{n,j}\rangle/\sqrt{d_{qk}} and before the softmax inside the modified Qwen forward pass; the unrescaled zn,jz_{n,j} that the gap-counting analysis reads is the score before this multiplier and softmax are applied. Dynamic-NTK RoPE is the upstream Qwen schedule with the per-nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}} base rescale of Peng et al. (2023, §3.4), controlled by Qwen’s existing use_dynamic_ntk configuration switch. The nanoGPT-side modification is a single length-nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}} per-position scalar vector βn\beta_{n} initialised to one and trained jointly with the rest of the model; the per-(layer, head) affine βn,ℓ,h=sℓ,h​βn+bℓ,h\beta_{n,\ell,h}=s_{\ell,h}\beta_{n}+b_{\ell,h} then folds into the attention computation as in (A.1).

Appendix B Detailed protocols and aggregate numerics for the ξβ\xi_{\beta}-sweeps

This appendix records the body βn\beta_{n} regression-fit protocol and the training-time trajectory deferred from ??.

B.1 Learnable inverse-temperature vector: βn\beta_{n} regression-fit protocol and trajectory

The four-configuration training schedule and the per-(layer, head) realization (A.1) of the learnable vector βn\beta_{n} are as in ??. At each of the seven milestone checkpoints, we extract βn\beta_{n} (a length-10241024 vector) and fit the bias-free regression model βn=a1​(log⁡n)ξβ\beta_{n}=a_{1}(\log n)^{\xi_{\beta}} in two settings:

Domain Bias a2a_{2} ξβ\xi_{\beta} search
SSMax (Nakanishi, 2025) (= M1) n∈[1,1024]n\in[1,1024] free grid
Ours, grid (= M2) n∈{64,…,1024}n\in\{64,\ldots,1024\} ≡0\equiv 0 grid (step 0.050.05)
Ours, OLS slope n∈{64,128,…,1024}n\in\{64,128,\ldots,1024\} (six points) ≡0\equiv 0 continuous

The body figures ??, ?? use the grid version of Ours. ?? reports the M2 loss landscape on the same fine grid for all four runs at three training milestones; the rotary runs are added here only as a reference, since the body intentionally does not contrast positional encodings.

Why a2≡0a_{2}\equiv 0.

The per-(layer, head) realization (A.1) already places a layer-side scalar bias inside the inverse-temperature parameterization. A free a2a_{2} in the post-hoc fit would re-introduce that same bias on top, leaving ξβ\xi_{\beta} under-identified by the residual curvature of βn\beta_{n}. Empirically, on the trained checkpoints, M1 (a2a_{2} free) selects ξβ=1\xi_{\beta}=1 in only 3/28​(11%)3/28\;(11\%) snapshots and otherwise wanders the grid with no stable trend across iters; the bias absorbs the signal. Forcing a2≡0a_{2}\equiv 0 removes this absorption and lets ξβ\xi_{\beta} identify the residual log-log slope of βn\beta_{n}.

Why n≥64n\geq 64.

The trimming threshold matches the smallest nn used by the body’s gap-counting estimator ξ^Λ\hat{\xi}_{\Lambda} of ??, ??, namely n=64n=64 (the smallest of the six nn values in ??). Defining ξ^β\hat{\xi}_{\beta} on the same domain makes the comparison with ξ^Λ\hat{\xi}_{\Lambda} direct rather than a domain-mismatch artefact; the residual finite-nn gap |ξ^Λ−ξ^β||\hat{\xi}_{\Lambda}-\hat{\xi}_{\beta}| is the value reported per cell in ??. The first half of the context length n≤50n\leq 50 also contains the small-nn dynamics of βn\beta_{n} that deviate from the asymptotic power family; trimming there isolates the scaling regime that ?? characterizes.

Trim sensitivity.

?? reports ξ^β\hat{\xi}_{\beta} as the trim threshold varies, on the two absolute-PE runs at iter=100​k\mathrm{iter}=100\mathrm{k}. The n≥64n\geq 64 choice sits in a stable plateau (within ±0.04\pm 0.04 of the n≥51n\geq 51 value), and pushing the threshold to n≥200n\geq 200 shifts ξ^β\hat{\xi}_{\beta} by ≤0.16\leq 0.16 on the more sensitive dataset (OpenWebText), consistent with βn\beta_{n} being well approximated by the power family on the asymptotic tail.

(SE on PPL ≤10%\leq 10\% of the cell mean in (a, b); half-IQR on MSE ≤8%\leq 8\% of the point-estimate MSE in (c, d)) are derived by the protocol below. Appendix C Auxiliary results for the deterministic theory

This appendix collects strands deferred from ??. ?? reduces the supremum (4.3) defining Λn\Lambda_{n} to a finite maximum over competitor gaps. ?? handles the degenerate case of ties at the maximum. ?? gives the score-realizability reduction used throughout ??: any positive score matrix arises from self-attention with Qn=KnQ_{n}=K_{n}.

Throughout this appendix we write 𝒰n:={zn∗−zn,j:1≤j≤n,zn,j<zn∗}\mathcal{U}_{n}:=\{z_{n}^{*}-z_{n,j}:1\leq j\leq n,\ z_{n,j}<z_{n}^{*}\} for the set of positive competitor gaps.

C.1 Discrete representation of Λn\Lambda_{n}

Lemma C.1 (Discrete representation of Λn\Lambda_{n}).

On the finite-Λn\Lambda_{n} domain (Nn​(0)=1N_{n}(0)=1), the upper-tail accumulation scale of ?? satisfies

Λn=supt>0log⁡Nn​(t)t=maxu∈𝒰n⁡log⁡Nn​(u)u.\Lambda_{n}=\sup_{t>0}\frac{\log N_{n}(t)}{t}=\max_{u\in\mathcal{U}_{n}}\frac{\log N_{n}(u)}{u}.

If Nn​(0)≥2N_{n}(0)\geq 2 (ties at the maximum), then Λn=∞\Lambda_{n}=\infty.

Proof.

C.3 Score realizability via positive Gram matrices

Definition C.3 (Positive matrix).

A matrix A∈ℝn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is positive semidefinite if x⊤​A​x≥0x^{\top}Ax\geq 0 for every x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. We call AA positive, and write A≥0A\geq 0, if AA is symmetric and positive semidefinite. Every Gram matrix considered in the sequel is positive in this sense, so we use the predicate A≥0A\geq 0 throughout.

Proposition C.4 (Gram reduction for positive score matrices).

Let Σn∈ℝn×n\Sigma_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} satisfy Σn≥0\Sigma_{n}\geq 0 with rank⁡Σn≤dqk,n\rank\Sigma_{n}\leq d_{\mathrm{qk},n}. Then there exist matrices Qn,Kn∈ℝdqk,n×nQ_{n},K_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{qk},n}\times n} with Qn=KnQ_{n}=K_{n} such that the self-attention score matrix equals Σn\Sigma_{n}:

⟨qn,i,kn,j⟩dqk,n=(Σn)i​j,1≤i,j≤n.\frac{\langle q_{n,i},k_{n,j}\rangle}{\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{qk},n}}}=(\Sigma_{n})_{ij},\qquad 1\leq i,j\leq n.

In particular, every row of Σn\Sigma_{n} is realized as a fixed-query self-attention score vector.

Proof.

Choose Bn∈ℝdqk,n×nB_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{qk},n}\times n} with Bn⊤​Bn=ΣnB_{n}^{\top}B_{n}=\Sigma_{n}, padding by zero rows if necessary. Setting Qn=Kn=dqk,n1/4​BnQ_{n}=K_{n}=d_{\mathrm{qk},n}^{1/4}B_{n} gives Qn⊤​Kn/dqk,n=Bn⊤​Bn=ΣnQ_{n}^{\top}K_{n}/\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{qk},n}}=B_{n}^{\top}B_{n}=\Sigma_{n}. ∎

The body’s TE scale Λn\Lambda_{n} controls the top-two/entropy pair via ?? but does not by itself imply coordinate-wise rank collapse (??). This appendix records the exact rank-collapse criterion, defines the corresponding rank boundary, identifies the positive-resolution accumulation proxy that sandwiches it, and proves ??.

Define the rank free energy

ℱn​(β):=log⁡Zn​(β).\mathcal{F}_{n}(\beta):=\log Z_{n}(\beta). (D.1)
Proposition D.1 (Exact coordinate-wise rank-collapse criterion).

Let

𝒢n​(β):=maxi,j⁡|pn,i​(β)−pn,j​(β)|.\mathcal{G}_{n}(\beta):=\max_{i,j}\bigl|p_{n,i}(\beta)-p_{n,j}(\beta)\bigr|.

For any positive deterministic sequence (βn)(\beta_{n}),

𝒢n(βn)→0⟺ℱn(βn)→∞.\mathcal{G}_{n}(\beta_{n})\to 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal{F}_{n}(\beta_{n})\to\infty.

Equivalently,

maxj|pn,j(βn)−1n|→0⟺ℱn(βn)→∞.\max_{j}\left|p_{n,j}(\beta_{n})-\frac{1}{n}\right|\to 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal{F}_{n}(\beta_{n})\to\infty.
Proof.

The largest unnormalised softmax weight equals 11, so

pn∗​(β):=maxj⁡pn,j​(β)=1Zn​(β)=e−ℱn​(β).p_{n}^{*}(\beta):=\max_{j}p_{n,j}(\beta)=\frac{1}{Z_{n}(\beta)}=e^{-\mathcal{F}_{n}(\beta)}.

pn∗​(β)≤𝒢n​(β)+1n.p_{n}^{*}(\beta)\leq\mathcal{G}_{n}(\beta)+\frac{1}{n}.

The coordinate-wise uniform-law equivalence follows from

pn∗(β)→0⟺maxj|pn,j(β)−1n|→0,p_{n}^{*}(\beta)\to 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\max_{j}\left|p_{n,j}(\beta)-\frac{1}{n}\right|\to 0,

because 1/n→01/n\to 0 and 0≤pn,j​(β)≤pn∗​(β)0\leq p_{n,j}(\beta)\leq p_{n}^{*}(\beta). ∎

Definition D.2 (Rank boundary).

For 0≤r≤log⁡n0\leq r\leq\log n, define

Bnrank​(r):=sup{β≥0:ℱn​(β)≥r}.B_{n}^{\mathrm{rank}}(r):=\sup\bigl\{\beta\geq 0:\mathcal{F}_{n}(\beta)\geq r\bigr\}.

βn≤Bnrank​(rn)\beta_{n}\leq B_{n}^{\mathrm{rank}}(r_{n})

eventually.

For r≥0r\geq 0, define

Λn(r):=supt>0:log⁡Nn​(t)>rlog⁡Nn​(t)−rt,\Lambda_{n}^{(r)}:=\sup_{t>0:\,\log N_{n}(t)>r}\frac{\log N_{n}(t)-r}{t},

D.1 Empirical instances on the verification cells

The verification cells of ?? occupy two distinct regimes of ??.

TE-to-RE upgrade.

?? identifies Λn\Lambda_{n} as the TE scale unconditionally; the upgrade to RE scale via ?? requires the contact-count entropy Cn=αn​log⁡nC_{n}=\alpha_{n}\log n to diverge, equivalently ξα>−1\xi_{\alpha}>-1. The four nanoGPT cells of ?? have ξ^α∈(−1.04,−0.86)\hat{\xi}_{\alpha}\in(-1.04,-0.86), so the relaxed condition holds with 1+ξ^α>01+\hat{\xi}_{\alpha}>0 giving a slow Cn≍(log⁡n)1+ξ^αC_{n}\asymp(\log n)^{1+\hat{\xi}_{\alpha}} divergence. The four Qwen cells have ξ^α∈(−1.69,−1.40)\hat{\xi}_{\alpha}\in(-1.69,-1.40) on the observed window; since Cn≥log⁡2C_{n}\geq\log 2 always, the bucket-mean slope ξ^α<−1\hat{\xi}_{\alpha}<-1 cannot persist asymptotically, and the analytical RE-scale upgrade of ?? does not directly apply, with the rank-resolved boundary of ?? as the formal substitute. The empirical boundary character of Λn\Lambda_{n} on these cells is then verified directly below.

Boundary check on Λn\Lambda_{n}.

Independently of the analytical sufficient condition, the boundary character of Λn\Lambda_{n} can be tested by reading the per-row maximum softmax weight pn∗​(β)=1/Zn​(β)p_{n}^{*}(\beta)=1/Z_{n}(\beta) at β=γ​Λn\beta=\gamma\Lambda_{n} on a sweep around criticality. ?? reports the median pn∗p_{n}^{*} at γ∈{0.5,1.0,1.5}\gamma\in\{0.5,1.0,1.5\} and the per-cell fraction of rows with pn∗≤1/log⁡np_{n}^{*}\leq 1/\log n at γ=0.1\gamma=0.1 (strict subcritical) on the four Qwen cells. Across all cells the median traces a smooth monotone curve from ∼10−3\sim 10^{-3} at γ=0.1\gamma=0.1 to ∼1\sim 1 at γ=4\gamma=4, crossing ∼0.42\sim 0.42 at γ=1\gamma=1, with ∼90%\sim 90\% of rows below 1/log⁡n1/\log n at γ=0.1\gamma=0.1 and 0%0\% at γ≥1\gamma\geq 1. The framework’s Λn\Lambda_{n} separates the subcritical-collapse regime from the supercritical-concentration regime empirically, including on the Qwen cells where the contact- count entropy is bounded and ?? does not directly apply. ?? shows that this analytical upgrade is sharp in the worst case (a contrived score family with CnC_{n} bounded fails rank collapse), but the Qwen rows in the bounded- CnC_{n} regime do not realize that pathology at the operating β\beta.

Appendix E Derivation of the YaRN inverse-temperature scaling

This appendix spells out why the YaRN context-window extension of Peng et al. (2023) produces an effective inverse-temperature scaling βn≍(log⁡n)2\beta_{n}\asymp(\log n)^{2}, i.e. implicit exponent ξ=2\xi=2 in the parameterisation of ??.

Peng et al. (2023) replace the standard softmax logit qm⊤​kn/dq_{m}^{\top}k_{n}/\sqrt{d} with qm⊤​kn/(t​d)q_{m}^{\top}k_{n}/(t\sqrt{d}) for a length-dependent temperature t=t⁡(s)t=t(s), where s=n/ntrains=n/n_{\mathrm{train}} is the ratio of the target context length nn to the training window ntrainn_{\mathrm{train}}. The recommended schedule (their §3.3) is

1t⁡(s)= 1+0.1​ln⁡s,\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{t(s)}}\;=\;1+0.1\,\ln s,

and the multiplier 1/t⁡(s)1/\sqrt{t(s)} is multiplied onto the rotary embeddings of both the query and the key. Substituting into the logit gives a rescaling

βn∝ 1/t⁡(n/ntrain)=(1+0.1​ln⁡(n/ntrain))2≍(log⁡n)2,\beta_{n}\;\propto\;1/t(n/n_{\mathrm{train}})\;=\;\bigl(1+0.1\ln(n/n_{\mathrm{train}})\bigr)^{2}\;\asymp\;(\log n)^{2},

i.e. a scalar multiplier ≍(log⁡n)2\asymp(\log n)^{2} asymptotically. The fact that the multiplier is applied to both sides of the inner product, rather than once, is what doubles the exponent relative to a log⁡n\log n-only temperature, and places YaRN in the ξ=2\xi=2 row of ??.

Appendix F Training-time exponent measurement: acquisition protocol, per-seed granularity, and limitations

This appendix gives the per-row gap-counting acquisition protocol, the βn\beta_{n} regression-fit protocol, and limitations for the training-time consistency check of ??. The upstream training setup that produces the learnable inverse-temperature vector βn\beta_{n} being measured here, namely the models, datasets, four-configuration schedule, and the per-(layer, head) realization (A.1), is documented in ??; the body βn\beta_{n} regression fit itself is in ??.

Gap-counting estimator ξ^Λ\hat{\xi}_{\Lambda}.

We analyse the four training-time GPT-124M runs (two PE datasets, two RoPE) of ?? at the seven milestone checkpoints. For each checkpoint, three evaluation seeds produce independent validation batches (B=16B=16 sequences, context lengths n∈{64,128,256,512,768,1024}n\in\{64,128,256,512,768,1024\}, block size 10241024). For each (layer, head, nn, batch) row we record the current-layer dot product zn,j=⟨q,kj⟩/dz_{n,j}=\langle q,k_{j}\rangle/\sqrt{d} with zn∗:=maxj⁡zn,jz^{*}_{n}:=\max_{j}z_{n,j}. Per-row Λn\Lambda_{n} and the contact coordinates (αn,Δn)(\alpha_{n},\Delta_{n}) are computed from ?? via the competitor gaps zn∗−zn,jz^{*}_{n}-z_{n,j} at numerical tolerance ϵ=10−6\epsilon=10^{-6}. The body’s ξ^Λ\hat{\xi}_{\Lambda} is the bucket-mean slope estimator of ??: rows are pooled across evaluation seeds into the index sets ℛ⁡(c,n)\mathcal{R}(c,n), the bucket mean is taken over those pooled rows at each of the six nn values, and ξ^Λ\hat{\xi}_{\Lambda} is the OLS slope of those bucket means against log⁡log⁡n\log\log n. Because each of the three seeds contributes the same (ℓ,h,batch,n)(\ell,h,\text{batch},n) structure, the pooled-row slope coincides with the mean of three per-seed slopes; the body’s headline half-width is the bootstrap-IQR/2 over (s,ℓ,h)(s,\ell,h) tuples of ??. Rows with log10⁡Λn>5\log_{10}\Lambda_{n}>5 (exact-tie configurations) are dropped before averaging, matching the Qwen protocol of ??.

Bootstrap intervals.

For each cell cc let 𝒯⁡(c)\mathcal{T}(c) be the cell’s bootstrap-unit set: {(ℓ,h)}\{(\ell,h)\} on Qwen and {(s,ℓ,h)}\{(s,\ell,h)\} on nanoGPT, the latter pooled across the three evaluation seeds. Each draw selects |𝒯⁡(c)||\mathcal{T}(c)| tuples uniformly with replacement from 𝒯⁡(c)\mathcal{T}(c), recomputes the bucket-mean slope ξ^X​(c)\hat{\xi}_{X}(c) from the rows in ℛ⁡(c,n)\mathcal{R}(c,n) that belong to the drawn tuples (separately at each n∈𝒩⁡(c)n\in\mathcal{N}(c)), and the half-IQR over B=200B=200 such draws is the half-width reported in ??; tie % follows the same convention. The ξβ∗\xi_{\beta}^{*} column carries no interval on Qwen (0.50.5-grid PPL minimum) and the six-point OLS standard error of ξ^β\hat{\xi}_{\beta} on nanoGPT.

βn\beta_{n}-fit estimator ξ^β\hat{\xi}_{\beta}.

At every checkpoint βn\beta_{n} is read off the model state and fitted to the bias-free power family βn=a1​(log⁡n)ξβ\beta_{n}=a_{1}(\log n)^{\xi_{\beta}} at the same six nn that the gap-counting uses. The OLS slope of log⁡βn\log\beta_{n} on log⁡log⁡n\log\log n at those six points yields ξ^β\hat{\xi}_{\beta} (closed-form least squares, no grid). The shared domain matters: ?? predicts equality of ξ^Λ\hat{\xi}_{\Lambda} and ξ^β\hat{\xi}_{\beta} in the limit, but only when both estimators are read on the same nn set; this is the choice we make throughout. The bias-free constraint a2≡0a_{2}\equiv 0 is justified in ??.

Limitations.

The check is limited in two respects. (i) Single training seed per configuration. The ξ^Λ\hat{\xi}_{\Lambda} band is over three evaluation batches at fixed training seed; variation from initialisation and data ordering is not measured. ξ^β\hat{\xi}_{\beta} has no eval-seed variance by construction. (ii) Short context. With n≤1024n\leq 1024 the log-log dynamic range covers half a decade, which constrains the bucket-mean slope but leaves higher-order curvature unconstrained; this is part of why ξ^Λ\hat{\xi}_{\Lambda} and ξ^β\hat{\xi}_{\beta} retain a finite-nn gap.

Attention rows are collected from all 3232 layers and 3232 heads on PG19 and Proof-Pile-2 at context lengths neval∈{8192,16384,32768}n_{\mathrm{eval}}\in\{8192,16384,32768\}, with four context-length values per document at the ratios n/neval∈{1/4,1/2,3/4,1}n/n_{\mathrm{eval}}\in\{1/4,1/2,3/4,1\} and one query position per (layer, head, document, nn) tuple. The body’s per-nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}} fit of ?? skips neval=ntrain=8192n_{\mathrm{eval}}=n_{\mathrm{train}}=8192 (training window, no extrapolation). The upstream pass applies a length-dependent inverse-temperature multiplier βn∝(log⁡n)ξ0\beta_{n}\propto(\log n)^{\xi_{0}} at the seven values ξ0∈{0,0.5,1,1.5,2,2.5,3}\xi_{0}\in\{0,0.5,1,1.5,2,2.5,3\}, where ξ0=0\xi_{0}=0 disables the multiplier; ξ0\xi_{0} perturbs the representation entering a layer while the measured object is always the unrescaled current-layer score zn,j=⟨𝐪n,in,𝐤n,j⟩/dq​kz_{n,j}=\langle\mathbf{q}_{n,i_{n}},\mathbf{k}_{n,j}\rangle/\sqrt{d_{qk}}. Across the three context lengths and four ratios, this yields eight values n∈{2048,4096,6144,8192,12288,16384,24576,32768}n\in\{2048,4096,6144,8192,12288,16384,24576,32768\}. The published-paper headline aggregation (??, ??) uses the document subset 44 from PG-19 and 55 from Proof-Pile-2, so the total attention-row count entering the headline statistics is 32×32×3​(neval)×4​(ratios)×7​(ξ0)×(4+5)​(docs)=774,144.32\times 32\times 3\,(n_{\mathrm{eval}})\times 4\,(\text{ratios})\times 7\,(\xi_{0})\times(4{+}5)\,(\text{docs})=774{,}144. The empirical contact gap is the largest competitor gap uu satisfying log⁡Nn​(u)/u≥(1−ϵ)​Λn\log N_{n}(u)/u\geq(1-\epsilon)\,\Lambda_{n} at ϵ=10−6\epsilon=10^{-6}, a floating-point relaxation of the exact maximizer in ??.

Per-nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}} fit.

The body ξ^pool​(neval)\hat{\xi}_{\rm pool}(n_{\mathrm{eval}}) is the OLS slope of the count-weighted means of log⁡Λn\log\Lambda_{n} taken at each of the four nn values within an nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}}, regressed against log⁡log⁡n\log\log n. Sink-token attention rows with log10⁡Λn>5\log_{10}\Lambda_{n}>5 are excluded from the bulk before averaging. Aggregating across nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}} at shared nn mixes three dynamic-NTK RoPE rescale conditions (one per source nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}}) and biases the slope; per-nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}} fits avoid this contamination.
